speaker: Zach Perret
title: How Plaid Survived on K Before Becoming Fintech Infrastructure | Zach Perret
question: Why would a late-stage private tech company with improving fundamentals and plenty of cash still take a down round?
guest: The underlying reality is market multiples have changed massively. You look at public companies, they've gone down hugely since that period of time, private companies as well. And so we ended up landing in what we think is a very rational valuation on top of a much better business. But the market multiples have changed, and that's why we had the step down in price. The interesting thing is we actually didn't need capital. I wouldn't have gone to raise capital, except that we had RSUs expiring, which means we needed to flip the RSUs into shares so that our employees could retain that value. We ended up not adding much capital to the balance sheet at all in that transaction. It also helps to have a more recent mark to market, so that when we're making an offer to a new executive, they can look and say, "Yeah, this is the price that was just paid by investors, and I understand that price."

points.core: Compressed market multiples lower private valuations even when underlying business metrics improve.
points.note: Accept: public or private comparable multiple contraction causing a lower price despite stronger revenue or fundamentals. Do not credit: blaming poor company performance or burning cash.

points.core: Expiring employee RSUs force a liquidity transaction to convert grants into shares.
points.note: Accept: double-trigger or time-expiring RSUs requiring a share conversion or tender so staff do not lose earned equity. Do not credit: vague mentions of keeping employees happy without citing RSU expiration or conversion.

points.core: A recent investor-priced valuation makes equity offers more credible to prospective executives.
points.note: Accept: current mark-to-market pricing helping senior hires trust and underwrite their compensation package. Do not credit: generic claims that fair valuations improve morale without linking to recruiting or offers.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Usually because the old valuation, not the business, is the problem. A price set at a market peak (say, 2021 multiples) can stay out of reach even as revenue and margins improve, and carrying that stale number creates real costs that a reset fixes.

The biggest is talent: employees hold options with strike prices above what the stock is realistically worth, so equity stops retaining or attracting people. A lower priced round, often paired with a new 409A valuation and repriced or refreshed grants, makes equity compensation meaningful again. Stripe's 2023 round at roughly half its peak valuation is the classic case; it raised largely to cover tax bills on expiring employee RSUs and provide liquidity, not to fund operations.

Other motives include setting a credible mark ahead of an IPO so the listing does not price below the last private round, bringing in a strategic or long-term investor who will only come in at a realistic price, enabling tender offers or stock-based acquisitions at a believable price, and raising from a position of strength rather than later under pressure. Anti-dilution and ratchet terms make this costly, so it is a deliberate trade-off.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Even with ample cash and improving fundamentals, a late-stage tech company may carry an outdated peak-era valuation after public market multiples compress. Often, the primary driver for a voluntary down round is talent retention and employee liquidity, as seen with Stripe in 2023. Long-tenured employees frequently hold restricted stock units approaching expiration, while underwater options and unattainable paper valuations hurt recruiting. Raising capital at a reset valuation lets the company fund tender offers, cover steep tax-withholding obligations on expiring RSUs without draining operating cash, and issue fresh equity grants with realistic upside.

A clean down round also clears valuation overhang before going public. Establishing credible price discovery with institutional crossover investors avoids a stigmatized "down IPO" later and sidesteps structured flat rounds laden with punitive liquidation preferences or ratchets that distort the cap table. Finally, repricing shares to reflect current market conditions can bring strategic partners onto the cap table or build dedicated firepower for opportunistic acquisitions while competitors remain capital-constrained.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Usually because the old valuation has become a liability, even though the business itself is fine. Many late-stage companies were priced at peak 2021 revenue multiples. Even with better growth and margins, comparable public companies now trade far lower, so the business can't "grow into" the old price fast enough.

A down round fixes several problems at once. It resets the price of employee equity. Underwater options and RSUs don't keep people around, while a realistic 409A valuation and repriced grants do. It also creates liquidity. Stripe's 2023 raise at about $50 billion, down from $95 billion, mostly paid employees' tax bills on expiring RSUs and funded share buybacks rather than operations. And it sets up a credible IPO. Taking the markdown privately avoids a "down IPO," IPO ratchets that kick in below a set price, and a messy public debut. Finally, a clear market price cleans up the cap table. It lets the company buy back stock, do deals using its shares as currency, and stop investors and staff from speculating about what the stock is really worth.

In short, the money matters less than the reset.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Even a cash-rich, fundamentally strong late-stage company may take a down round to solve structural problems created by an inflated peak-market valuation. Most commonly, it enables employee liquidity and tax coverage: long-tenured staff often hold expiring stock options or vesting RSUs with hefty tax bills, and raising capital for a tender offer satisfies those obligations without depleting operating cash. Resetting the valuation also lowers the 409A strike price, making new equity grants attractive again for hiring and retention.

A down round can also clear a valuation overhang ahead of an eventual IPO. When public-market multiples compress, clinging to an outdated private mark deters crossover investors and sets up a painful down-IPO. Accepting a lower, realistic price lets the company bring in marquee institutional backers, give fatigued early investors partial exits, or build an M&A war chest—all while keeping clean deal terms rather than hiding a flat headline valuation behind punitive liquidation preferences or ratchets.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A down round reflects what investors will pay today compared with what they paid in the last round. A company can grow revenue, improve margins, and burn less cash while its valuation falls. The previous round may have been priced in a hotter market, and comparable public companies may now trade at lower multiples.

Plenty of cash gives management the option to wait. Taking the round anyway can make sense if it brings in a valuable investor, funds an acquisition or expansion, or gives the company enough runway to choose when to go public. A lower price with straightforward terms can also be cheaper for existing shareholders than preserving the headline valuation by giving new investors a larger guaranteed payout in a sale. The decision comes down to whether those benefits outweigh the dilution and any rights triggered by the lower share price.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A company can be doing better than it was at its last round and still be worth less in today’s market. The last valuation may have been set when investors paid more for each dollar of revenue or expected faster growth. Even rising revenue and shrinking losses may not be enough to justify that price today.

Plenty of cash gives management a choice. If an IPO could take years, raising now can fund expansion or an acquisition and reduce the risk of having to raise later on worse terms. A lower valuation can also be a better deal for founders and employees than preserving the old headline price by promising new investors a larger share of the proceeds in a sale. Existing holders accept dilution because the added flexibility and cleaner terms can be worth more than defending the old valuation.
